speaker: David Chang
title: Chef David Chang (Momofuku): “I’m Addicted to Creative Excitement”
question: In an independent restaurant group, why do creative founders often keep launching new concepts even when it hurts the business?
guest: When we tried a lot of things earlier, we didn't have investors. We're all self-funded. And I was, in many ways, feeding my own ego, and I thought what my own ego wanted was what everybody else wanted, and that wasn't clearly a good move. Indulging in what I wanna do has its positives, clearly, but more often it's an addiction to doing something creatively. During the pandemic, I wanted to open up restaurant after restaurant after restaurant. Part of knowing addiction—and I'm an addict to work, I'm an addict to that creative excitement—is knowing that I need someone else to keep me accountable. So stepping down from day-to-day decision-making rights and entrusting Marguerite Mariscal as CEO, who prevents me from doing whatever I wanna do, has been the best decision for everybody. She's like, 'No, we're not doing that. We'll do it if it follows these things that we need.' ... Not distractions that are good for the moment. Maybe not good three, four, five years down the road. Again, maybe good for me, maybe not good for anybody else.

points.core: Founders mistake feeding personal ego for what everyone else wants.
points.note: Accept: conflating personal ego/desires with what the business, team, or customers actually need. Do not credit: blaming poor market research or lack of culinary talent.

points.core: Founders become addicted to the rush of short-term creative excitement.
points.note: Accept: compulsive novelty-seeking or addiction to creative excitement that feels rewarding immediately even when harmful 3–5 years out. Do not credit: claiming founders expand purely for financial greed.

points.core: Unchecked founders lack an accountable operator holding real veto power.
points.note: Accept: self-funded/unchecked founders having no independent CEO or operator with day-to-day decision rights who can say 'no' unless strategic criteria are met. Do not credit: vague advice to 'be more disciplined' without structural accountability.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Mostly because the founder's motivation and the business's needs diverge once the first restaurant works. Creative founders are energized by invention: designing a menu, a room, and a story. Running a mature restaurant is the opposite kind of work, built on repetition, cost control, staffing, and consistency. A new concept is a way back to the part of the job they love and are best at, and away from the operational grind they find draining.

Several forces reinforce this. Their identity and reputation rest on being creators, and press, awards, and guest buzz reward openings, not steady margins. New projects also feel like progress and can mask problems in existing units, since growth brings fresh investor money, landlord deals, and opening-month revenue. Opportunities keep arriving (a great space, a talented chef who needs a promotion path to stay), and each looks compelling on its own. Meanwhile, founders tend to be overconfident that past success will transfer, and few people in the group have the standing to say no.

The cost is that each distinct concept adds complexity without scale economies, spreading leadership attention, cash, and talent thinner.

points.why: The response describes a conflict between the founder’s preferences and the business’s needs without showing that the founder mistakes those preferences for what others want.
The response explains why invention is more appealing than routine operations but stops short of describing a compulsive pursuit of the short-term creative rush.
The response says few people have the standing to object but does not establish that the founder lacks an accountable operator with authority to veto launches.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Creative restaurant founders are typically wired for invention rather than maintenance, drawing energy and identity from designing menus, spaces, and opening-night experiences while finding the repetitive discipline of margin management and operational standardization draining. External incentives reinforce that impulse: dining media, awards, and landlords offering generous build-out deals disproportionately reward novelty over steady execution, while outside investors are often easier to attract to an exciting new project than to an aging flagship. Internally, constant concept creation also functions as a retention tool, giving ambitious chefs and managers their own venues to run so they do not leave to become competitors. Financially, new openings can create a seductive illusion of momentum, as fresh investor capital and honeymoon revenue spikes temporarily mask eroding same-store sales or thin unit margins at existing locations. Yet because every one-off concept demands distinct sourcing, training, marketing, and executive attention—unlike replicating a proven model—each launch forfeits economies of scale and dilutes leadership focus, quietly compounding overhead and operational fragility across the entire group.

points.why: The response says founders draw identity from invention but never says they mistake their own desires for what the business, team, or customers need.
The response describes a preference for invention and its operational costs without showing that the immediate creative rush drives compulsive launches.
The response identifies diluted leadership focus but never links repeated launches to the absence of an operator with authority to veto them.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Founders usually launch concepts because creating is what they're good at and what they enjoy, while running mature restaurants is a different job. Opening something new brings novelty, press attention, industry status, and a clear sense of identity. Making an existing store's margins better is slow, unglamorous work, and the founder often doesn't enjoy it or isn't skilled at it.

Several pressures add to this. Each new opening feels like growth, even when the existing restaurants are underperforming. A new concept can also be a way to escape a struggling one instead of fixing it. Investors, landlords offering deals, and talented staff who want promotions can all push for expansion.

There's also a blind spot. Founders tend to undercount the hidden costs, including spread-out management attention, weaker systems, team burnout, lost purchasing scale across different menus, and drift in quality at the flagship. These costs show up slowly, while the excitement of an opening is immediate.

Without a strong operating partner or a board to impose discipline, the founder's instincts end up setting the strategy.

points.why: The response identifies status and identity as personal rewards but never says founders mistake those desires for what the business, team, or customers need.
The response describes the immediate thrill of opening and the delayed costs without establishing that the thrill becomes a compulsion that drives repeated launches.
The response attributes founder-driven strategy to the absence of an operator or board with the authority to impose constraints.
quotes: Without a strong operating partner or a board to impose discipline, the founder's instincts end up setting the strategy.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Creative founders in independent restaurant groups often keep launching new concepts because the thrills that drive them—ideating menus, designing spaces, and chasing opening-night buzz—are fundamentally different from the repetitive discipline of running mature restaurants. Once a venue settles into routine operations, restless chefs and restaurateurs frequently seek a fresh creative outlet rather than focusing on incremental margin optimization.

Financial and organizational incentives reinforce this habit. New concepts attract outside investor capital, landlord tenant-improvement allowances, and renewed press attention, generating short-term cash inflows that can temporarily mask thinning profitability at older locations. Opening new doors is also a common way to retain ambitious chefs and managers who would otherwise leave without a path to leadership or equity. Finally, early acclaim breeds overconfidence, while rare real estate opportunities trigger a fear of missing out. Together, these psychological and structural pressures pull founders into chronic expansion even as it stretches leadership thin, drains working capital, and erodes the core business.

points.why: The response mentions overconfidence but never says founders mistake their personal desires for what the business, team, or customers want.
The response identifies the immediate creative thrill as a driver of repeated launches despite damage to the business.
quotes: restless chefs and restaurateurs frequently seek a fresh creative outlet
pull founders into chronic expansion even as it stretches leadership thin, drains working capital, and erodes the core business

points.why: The response discusses organizational incentives but never identifies the absence of an operator with authority to veto new concepts.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Opening restaurants is often what made the founders successful. A new concept lets them do the work they love: imagine a room, build a menu, and bring a team together. Opening night gives them immediate feedback from guests, staff, and the press. Improving margins or developing managers takes longer, and the payoff is less visible. When an existing restaurant starts to struggle, a new opening can feel like the fastest way to regain momentum.

The costs show up across the group. A launch can pull the strongest managers out of established restaurants, absorb their cash, and divert the founders’ attention just when those restaurants need it. A packed opening tells the founders people wanted to try the concept. It can take months to learn whether guests will return often enough to cover the costs, and by then the next lease may already be signed.

points.why: The response describes what founders enjoy but never says they mistake their own desires for what others need.
The response explains the appeal of immediate feedback and renewed momentum without showing that the rush of creating something new becomes compulsive.
The response describes the costs of expansion but does not attribute repeated launches to the absence of an operator with veto power.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
For many creative founders, inventing a restaurant is the part of the job they love and do best. A new concept gives them a chance to try an idea, draws attention, and can feel like progress. Making an existing restaurant consistently profitable takes a different kind of work. Better scheduling or less food waste rarely brings the recognition of an opening.

The rewards of launching are immediate and personal, while the costs emerge gradually across the group. An opening can absorb cash, pull a trusted manager away from a busy dining room, and stretch the founder’s attention just as the older restaurants need it. If the founder has the final say and no one can insist that the group has the cash and people to support another opening, the next idea can win even when the business would benefit more from a year of steady operation.

points.why: The response identifies personal rewards but never says founders mistake their own desires for what others want or the business needs.
The response explains the immediate appeal of launching and its delayed costs without establishing that the pursuit of creative excitement becomes compulsive.
The response makes the founder’s unchecked decision authority a cause of openings that proceed without someone empowered to enforce resource requirements.
quotes: the founder has the final say and no one can insist that the group has the cash and people to support another opening
